questions.stem: The melting points of three related compounds are $\begin{array}{l l} \mathrm {c a p r i c a c i d} & 3 2 ^ {\circ} \mathrm {C} \\ \mathrm {f o r m i c a c i d} & 8 ^ {\circ} \mathrm {C} \\ \mathrm {p a l m i t i c a c i d} & 6 3 ^ {\circ} \mathrm {C} \end{array}$ The boiling point of all these compounds is above 100 $ ^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the grid to draw a bar chart of the melting points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Room temperature has been marked on the grid. Use your bar chart to give the physical state of each acid at room temperature.

questions.stem: A student produces this chromatogram for four dyes, A, B, C and D.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put a cross ( $ \times $ ) in a box to indicate your answer.

parts.label: a-i
parts.text: Which one of the dyes contains three colours? A B C D

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Which one of the dyes contains one colour only? A B C D

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each dye is made from one or more of the colours blue, red and yellow. The student thinks that the result for one dye is incorrect. Suggest which result is incorrect. Explain your answer. The incorrect result is because ...

questions.stem: The photograph shows an aeroplane that has a rocket motor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: One of the tanks on the aeroplane contains liquid oxygen.

parts.label: a-i
parts.text: Complete the diagram to show the arrangement of the particles in a liquid. One particle has been drawn for you.

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Much more oxygen can be stored in the tank when the oxygen is a liquid rather than a gas. Give a reason for this in terms of the arrangement of the particles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: State two observations that can be made when magnesium burns in oxygen.

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: Give the formula of magnesium oxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A small amount of magnesium oxide is dissolved in water. When universal indicator is added to this solution, the indicator turns blue.

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: What does the observation with the indicator show about magnesium oxide?

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Identify the ion that is responsible for the universal indicator turning blue.

questions.stem: An excess of dilute hydrochloric acid was added to a lump of calcium carbonate in a beaker. The mass of the beaker and contents was recorded every 30 seconds. The graph shows the results. Mass of beaker and contents in grams $\mathrm {C a C O} _ {3} (\mathrm {s}) + 2 \mathrm {H C l} (\mathrm {a q}) \rightarrow \mathrm {C a C l} _ {2} (\mathrm {a q}) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {I}) + \mathrm {C O} _ {2} (\mathrm {g})$ The equation for the reaction is

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two observations that can be made when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to calcium carbonate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the test for carbon dioxide gas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the mass of the beaker and contents, and the time. (1)

parts.label: d
parts.text: After how many minutes did the reaction stop?

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: State why the reaction eventually stopped.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Identify the compounds, other than water, present in the solution in the beaker (i) after two minutes

parts.label: e-ii
parts.text: after five minutes

parts.label: f
parts.text: The experiment was repeated using the same mass of calcium carbonate, but as a powder instead of a single lump. On the graph, sketch the curve you would expect to obtain from this second experiment.

questions.stem: Soluble salts can be made by reacting an acid with a metal hydroxide, a metal oxide, or a metal carbonate. Insoluble salts can be made by using a precipitation reaction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Complete the table to show which acid or metal compound is used to make each salt listed. For each metal compound, state whether it would be used as a solid or in aqueous solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An acid is a source of hydrogen ions, $ \mathrm{H}^{+} $ Write an equation to show the ions formed when sulfuric acid is dissolved in water.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lead(II) chloride is an insoluble salt that can be prepared by reacting lead(II) nitrate with sodium chloride. Describe how you would prepare a pure, dry sample of lead(II) chloride starting from solid lead(II) nitrate and solid sodium chloride.

questions.stem: This is a recipe for making plum wine. Dissolve 1.5 kg of sugar in 5 dm $ ^{3} $ of warm water. Add yeast and 8 kg of plums. Pour the mixture into a flask. Leave the flask for several weeks until the reaction has stopped. Remove the solid yeast and pour the clear liquid into bottles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sugar contains sucrose, $ C_{1 2} H_{2 2} O_{1 1} $ When yeast is added, water reacts with sucrose to form glucose, $ \mathrm{C_{6} H_{1 2} O_{6}} $ Write a chemical equation for this reaction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The glucose is then converted into ethanol by the yeast $\mathrm {C} _ {6} \mathrm {H} _ {1 2} \mathrm {O} _ {6} (\mathrm {a q}) \rightarrow 2 \mathrm {C} _ {2} \mathrm {H} _ {5} \mathrm {O H} (\mathrm {a q}) + 2 \mathrm {C O} _ {2} (\mathrm {g})$

parts.label: b-i
parts.text: How would you know when the reaction has stopped?

parts.label: b-ii
parts.text: How could the solid yeast be removed from the mixture?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ethanol can be converted into chloroethene, $ \mathrm{C H_{2}=C H C l} $ , in three stages. Stage 1 Ethanol is dehydrated to form ethene, $ \mathrm{C H_{2}=C H_{2}} $ Stage 2 Ethene is converted into 1,2-dichloroethane, $ \mathrm{C H_{2} C I C H_{2} C I} $ Stage 3 1,2-dichloroethane is converted into chloroethene and hydrogen chloride

parts.label: c-i
parts.text: Why is the reaction in Stage 1 described as dehydration?

parts.label: c-ii
parts.text: Identify the catalyst used in the reaction in Stage 1.

parts.label: c-iii
parts.text: Suggest the name or formula of the substance used to react with ethene in Stage 2.

parts.label: c-iv
parts.text: Write a chemical equation for the reaction in Stage 3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Chloroethene can be used to make the polymer poly(chloroethene), also known as PVC. The displayed formula for part of the PVC molecule is

parts.label: d-i
parts.text: Draw a displayed formula for a chloroethene molecule.

parts.label: d-ii
parts.text: Describe, in terms of structure and bonding, what happens when chloroethene molecules are converted into poly(chloroethene).

questions.stem: A student set up this apparatus to measure the volume of carbon dioxide given off when a sample of a carbonate of a Group 2 metal was reacted with dilute nitric acid. She weighed out some of the carbonate and put it in a conical flask. She then added an excess of dilute nitric acid. After adding the acid she placed the bung and delivery tube into the conical flask. She measured the total volume of gas collected at room temperature and pressure (rtp) in the measuring cylinder. Her results are shown in the table. The equation for the reaction is $\mathrm {X C O} _ {3} (\mathrm {s}) + 2 \mathrm {H N O} _ {3} (\mathrm {a q}) \rightarrow \mathrm {X} \left(\mathrm {N O} _ {3}\right) _ {2} (\mathrm {a q}) + \mathrm {H} _ {2} \mathrm {O} (\mathrm {l}) + \mathrm {C O} _ {2} (\mathrm {g})$ where X is the symbol for the Group 2 metal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount, in moles, of carbon dioxide gas collected. (Assume that one mole of gas has a volume of 24000 $ cm^{3} $ at rtp) Amount of carbon dioxide gas collected = mol

parts.label: a-ii
parts.text: Deduce the amount, in moles, of the carbonate that reacted.

parts.label: a-iii
parts.text: Using the mass of the carbonate and your answer to (a)(ii), calculate the relative formula mass $ ( M_{r} ) $ of this carbonate. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: a-iv
parts.text: Calculate a value for the relative atomic mass of the Group 2 metal, X, and use the Periodic Table on page 2 to suggest its identity. Relative atomic mass of X = ... Identity of X=.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After the student had completed the experiment she was told that the metal carbonate was calcium carbonate. She calculated that 0.888 g of calcium carbonate would produce $ 2 1 3 \mathrm{c m}^{3} $ of carbon dioxide. She was certain that she had measured the mass of the metal carbonate correctly. Suggest two reasons why the volume of gas she collected was less than $ 2 1 3 \mathrm{c m}^{3}. $
